name: Honey mask (manuka)

lead: A manuka honey mask is honey from the manuka tree spread on the face and rinsed off, used to calm irritated skin and clear breakouts for a clearer, calmer complexion.

Proponents point to methylglyoxal, the compound credited for manuka's activity, and to antibacterial effects seen in lab studies. Honey has been studied in wound care, including early evidence of faster healing of partial-thickness burns. No acne studies were found.

paras: People apply a thin layer of manuka honey to clean skin, leave it on for a short period, and rinse with warm water, often once or a few times a week. It is used on its own or as part of a gentle routine. Users usually judge it by how calm and clear skin looks over a few weeks.

Honey is generally safe in food amounts, and honey is advised against for babies. Labelling and authenticity of manuka products are disputed, and grading systems such as UMF and MGO vary. As with any food product on skin, allergic reactions or irritation are possible in people sensitive to honey or bee products.

angle.text: Skincare fans apply manuka honey as a rinse-off mask to calm skin and clear breakouts, citing its antibacterial activity. Honey has been studied in wound care; no acne studies were found.

lead: A manuka honey mask is mānuka honey spread over the face and left on before rinsing. People use it to calm breakouts, soften skin and give it a smoother, more hydrated look, and it is a staple of at-home skincare routines.

Mānuka honey is made from the nectar of Leptospermum scoparium, native to New Zealand and coastal Australia; its activity is attributed in part to methylglyoxal and graded by systems such as UMF and MGO. [1] A 2013 review in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology describes honey in skin care as an emollient, humectant and soothing ingredient found in cleansing milks, creams, lip products and masks, with antimicrobial activity attributed to hydrogen peroxide or, in manuka, methylglyoxal. [2]

Wikipedia describes the honey's marker compounds as leptosperin, lepteridine and 2'-methoxyacetophenone, alongside methylglyoxal (MGO), dihydroxyacetone (DHA), flavonoids and phenolics, and notes that it is mostly fructose and glucose [1]. The honey is very viscous, dark cream to dark brown, with a strong earthy flavour [1].

Laboratory work indicates manuka honey shows antibacterial effects even when hydrogen peroxide activity is blocked, and medical-grade honeys have been tested against resistant bacteria in vitro. [3] Wound-care trials in humans exist for honey; trials specifically of a manuka honey face mask for acne have not been published.

paras: Mānuka honey is a monofloral honey made by European honey bees from the nectar of the mānuka tree, Leptospermum scoparium, which grows wild in New Zealand and south-eastern Australia and flowers at the same time as kānuka, a plant that is hard to tell apart even for beekeepers [1]. Māori have long treated the tree as a taonga, using leaf infusions for colds and fevers and bark oils or poultices for wounds and skin conditions [1].

The 2013 dermatology review notes honey's use in cosmetic formulations at concentrations from about 1 to 10 percent, and up to 70 percent when mixed with oils, gels or emulsifiers. [2] It also records historical use of honey on skin across early civilizations and use in treatments for conditions such as seborrhea, dandruff and psoriasis. [2] A 2014 American Family Physician review of impetigo lists manuka honey among natural remedies reported as anecdotally successful, without enough evidence to recommend it. [4]

sections.h: How it is used in masks
paras: Face masks are made by spreading a layer of the honey on the face and rinsing it off after a while; users also wash with it or use raw honey as a scrub. Dermatology literature explains why honey is used this way: a 2013 review describes it as an emollient, humectant and soothing ingredient found in cleansing milks, creams, lip products and masks, and attributes antimicrobial activity to hydrogen peroxide or, in manuka honey, to methylglyoxal [2].

Mānuka honey is graded by methylglyoxal content (mg/kg) and by the trademarked UMF scale [1]. The UMF Honey Association says roughly six times more honey is sold internationally as mānuka than New Zealand produces, and UK tests in 2011-2013 found most mānuka-labelled samples lacked expected non-peroxide activity [1].

In New Zealand honey is graded by both MGO (mg/kg) and UMF (Unique Mānuka Factor); selected equivalences are 83 mg/kg MGO to UMF 5, 514 to UMF 15, 829 to UMF 20 and 1,450 to UMF 28 [1]. The UK uses MGO and non-peroxide activity (NPA), which is numerically close to UMF, while the K-factor counts pollen particles and does not correlate with an active chemical [1]. Since 5 January 2018 New Zealand's Ministry for Primary Industries has required honey to pass a five-attribute test (four chemical and one DNA marker) to be labelled as New Zealand mānuka [1]. The UMF Honey Association was formed in 2002 as the Active Mānuka Honey Association and renamed in 2011; the Australian Mānuka Honey Association, set up in 2017, requires at least 85 mg/kg MGO and 170 mg/kg DHA [1].

Wikipedia reports that only about 1,700 tonnes are produced in New Zealand each year while around six times that is marketed internationally as mānuka; tests by the UMF association in 2012-2013 found 43 of 73 samples from Britain, China and Singapore negative, and Hong Kong tests found 14 of 56 samples adulterated with syrup [1].

A 2011 review states that non-peroxide activity in manuka honey comes with low pH and high sugar content that hinder microbial growth, and that antimicrobial activity varies widely between honeys depending on nectar sources. [3] Trials of manuka honey in other settings, such as eyelid wound healing and nasal irrigation for sinusitis, have been published. [5][6]
A 2016 article in the Journal of Primary Health Care on manuka honey, titled 'Potion or Poison?', discusses the claims made about it [7].

Wikipedia reports preliminary evidence for faster burn healing, moderate evidence for post-operative wounds, and low-quality evidence for other wound types; several medical-grade honey products are FDA-approved for minor wounds and burns [8]. Honey is not recommended for infants under one year because of botulism risk [8].

No studies found on manuka honey face masks for acne or skin appearance. Honey has been studied in wound and burn care, where Wikipedia reports preliminary evidence for faster burn healing. [8] Randomized trials have tested manuka honey on eyelid wounds and in chronic rhinosinusitis irrigation. [5][6]

Randomized trials have tested manuka honey in other settings. A 2017 trial assessed manuka honey for eyelid wound healing [5]. A 2017 single-blinded randomized trial gave patients with active chronic rhinosinusitis and prior sinus surgery either manuka honey or saline sinus irrigation twice daily for 30 days [6]. A 2014 placebo-controlled trial tested manuka honey for radiation-induced oral mucositis [9], a 2018 trial compared honey with mupirocin for decolonising nasal MRSA [10], and a 2006 trial compared honey dressing with paraffin tulle gras after toenail surgery [11]. A randomized pilot trial of a gelatin, manuka honey and hydroxyapatite biomaterial examined healing of Mohs surgical defects [12]. None of these tested a face mask for acne or skin appearance.

Mānuka honey is promoted as a premium product and is described in media and marketing as 'liquid gold' [1]. Wikipedia reports New Zealand exports worth about NZ$446 million in 2020, more than 90 percent of the country's honey export earnings, falling to NZ$387 million by 2024 [1]. Between 2022 and 2025 the US FDA issued warning letters to four manufacturers, including one Australian company, for marketing mānuka products as eye therapies, and a fifth for an anti-allergic claim; the agency said the products were unapproved drugs with false health claims [1].

claims.claim: Washing and masking with raw or manuka honey gives soft, high-quality skin, even with acne scars.
Scrubbing with honey exfoliates and grows new skin layers.
Honey is a gentle cleanser that never dries the skin.
The higher the UMF or MGO rating, the better it works on the face.
